claims.text: A blog post titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ and covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK tied infrastructure to AWS.
Multi-cloud was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
SST was originally built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
AWS CDK and CloudFormation act as a code generator, producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources.
AWS CDK is AWS-only, while Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-prem.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python, whereas Pulumi supports any programming language.
AWS CDK deployments are slower due to CloudFormation, while Pulumi deploys faster via direct execution.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file, while Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK supports only AWS Secrets Manager for secrets management, while Pulumi supports cross-cloud secrets.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging while AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment rather than generating an intermediary format.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
Pulumi Insights product page provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities.
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments provides advanced deployment workflows.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies "day one" tasks, documented in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
An on-demand workshop titled "Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS" exists at pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, whose constructs/components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine and bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service, SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` needs no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account (self-hosted), not in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the framework's Ion-based rewrite.
The SST team has repeatedly said, about their own architecture, that SST is built on the Pulumi engine since the rewrite shipped.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST can deploy applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST users define app infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST components, and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024.
Ion (SST v3 architecture) has been the only supported SST architecture since its release.

The SST blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

The SST blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs 'What is SST' page says: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin's article 'Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis' says SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to SST constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to be defined and deployed.

Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article 'SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion' says: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published platform/package.json for SST depends on @pulumi/pulumi plus Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds, and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider (@pulumiverse/vercel).

The SST repository is at anomalyco/sst (formerly sst/sst), and platform/package.json lists @pulumi/pulumi, @pulumi/aws, @pulumi/cloudflare, @pulumi/command, @pulumi/docker-build, @pulumi/random, @pulumi/tls, and @pulumiverse/vercel as direct dependencies.

In SST deploys, components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph and orders operations, and Terraform-bridged providers translate each resource into cloud API calls.
Pulumi's engine provides dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
The Pulumi Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem for the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API lets teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools, working by embedding the engine without requiring Pulumi Cloud.
The Pulumi provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
The link targets /blog/any-terraform-provider/, /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/, /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/ exist.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework whose docs state "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.

Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, and its Pulumi provider (DefangLabs/pulumi-defang) is described as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`".
Nitric and Defang, like SST, run application deployments through the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer.
Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
Resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly in Pulumi inside an SST app and deployed as part of the same app, because SST constructs compile to Pulumi resources.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package is pulling roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 downloads for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
SST's own team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch and now has a larger following on GitHub (more stars) than SST itself.
The opencode work has not changed SST's release cadence or its dependency on the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state; policy as code provides guardrails enforced centrally; components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
SST doesn't invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state; its Terraform providers are bridged through the Pulumi engine.
SST doesn't expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across more than one application on its own.

Link targets /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/, /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/, /blog/any-terraform-provider/ and /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/ exist; the first is a fuller story of SST's move off CDK told from SST's side.
SST v3 dropped AWS CDK for an embedded Pulumi engine talking to Terraform-bridged providers, with no Pulumi account required.
